subject: Integration recap + recommended auth pattern for FinPulse POC
messages:
From: Logan Wright <logan.wright@redwood.com>
To: Ana Gomez <ana.gomez@finpulse.io>, Sam Patel <sam.patel@finpulse.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 30 Aug 2026 16:23:00 -0700
Subject: Integration recap + recommended auth pattern for FinPulse POC

Hi Ana / Sam —

Great call today, thanks for walking through your ingestion and routing needs. Below is a concise recap and our recommended auth + integration approach for the POC. I attached a short PDF with a comparison matrix (redwood-auth-options.pdf) and an initial checklist (initial-integration-checklist.xlsx).

Quick recap of what we heard from FinPulse:
- High-throughput embedding + reranker workload for search and personalization (peaks 500 req/s).
- Frontend clients (web/mobile) will call backend APIs; no direct public client->Redwood calls for now.
- Strict rotation and audit requirements; security wants short-lived credentials and KMS-backed keys.
- Multi-region routing for EU and US customers later in Q4.

Our recommended auth pattern (POC -> production):
1) Backend-to-Redwood (primary): Service account tokens + short-lived signing keys.
   - Create a named service account per environment (poe/poc, prod).
   - Use short-lived JWTs (15m-1h) minted by your auth service, signed with a key stored in your KMS/HSM; Redwood validates signatures and aud/iss.
   - Rotate signing keys regularly (recommended 30–90 days) — RBAC for key access.
2) Frontend -> Backend: keep the exchange on your side.
   - Frontends get short-lived session tokens from your auth system; your backend performs token exchange and calls Redwood with the service account JWT.
   - Avoid embedding long-lived API keys in client apps.
3) API keys for low-risk server-to-server integrations only (short TTL, single-purpose).
4) Embeddings / Reranker namespace: use scoped credentials (scopes: embeddings:write, embeddings:read, reranker:invoke) so you can audit per-feature usage.

Routing and model variants:
- We recommend model routing policy: route to lowest-cost compatible model for background batch embeds; route to higher-SLO variants for user-facing reranker calls.
- Use the Redwood SDK to tag traffic with a "feature" header (e.g., X-FP-Feature: search-rerank) so downstream dashboards separate costs.

Structured output & tool-calling:
- If you plan to use function/tool calling, enable explicit function schemas and sign tool definitions in your config. We'll validate tool definitions at ingest time.

Next steps / asks from FinPulse:
- Please share a high-level architecture diagram showing where the token exchange would live (auth service -> backend -> Redwood).
- Any compliance checklist items the security team wants included in the audit export (SOC2 sections, log retention windows).
- Confirm preferred time for a 60-min technical deep-dive with engineering + security.

Availability: we have Wed / Thu next week open for a deep-dive (9–11am PT or 2–4pm PT).

Thanks —

Logan Wright
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
logan.wright@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0124

Subject: Re: Integration recap + recommended auth pattern for FinPulse POC

Thanks, Logan — useful summary. A few follow-ups from our side:

1) Token-exchange flow: can you elaborate on what you mean by "short-lived JWTs minted by our auth service" versus Redwood issuing tokens? Our security lead prefers minimizing in-house token logic. Would Redwood provide a token broker or is the expectation that all signing lives on our side?

2) Embeddings/reranker isolation: what's the recommended pattern if we want separate billing and per-team quotas? Do we create separate service accounts or do you recommend scoping via namespaces/labels?

3) Routing across regions: we will be subject to EU data locality for some customers. How does Redwood handle routing + fallbacks with key validation across regions (e.g., if a request is validated in us-west and then routed to eu-central)?

4) Client-side concern: we are evaluating a lightweight on-device inference fallback for rare offline flows. If we ever allow client->Redwood direct calls, would Redwood support OAuth with PKCE and short-lived tokens? What are the security trade-offs you recommend?

Could Marissa or Logan confirm options 1 and 2 in more detail? Also looping in our security team (security@finpulse.io) for their input.

—Ana
Ana Gomez
VP Engineering, FinPulse
ana.gomez@finpulse.io | +1 (206) 555-0199

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Ana Gomez <ana.gomez@finpulse.io>, Sam Patel <sam.patel@finpulse.io>
Cc: Logan Wright <logan.wright@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 01 Sep 2026 08:37:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Integration recap + recommended auth pattern for FinPulse POC

Hi Ana —

Quick answers inline, plus a recommended configuration for your set-up.

1) Token broker: Redwood does not require you to build complex token brokers. Options: 
   - Option A (recommended for most customers): Your auth system mints short-lived, signed JWTs for service accounts; Redwood validates JWT signature + claims. This keeps the private signing key inside your KMS/HSM.
   - Option B (alternative): Redwood issues short-lived tokens via an API when authenticated by a long-lived, low-scope API key or using a mutually authenticated mTLS call from your backend. We can support that flow if you want Redwood to handle token minting for you (we log issuance in the audit trail).

Trade-offs: Option A keeps full control with FinPulse (recommended for sensitive controls). Option B reduces implementation work for you but requires trust of Redwood key issuance (we support audit exports and retention policies).

2) Embeddings/reranker separation: recommended approach for clear billing + quotas:
   - Create a unique service account per product surface (e.g., search-service-account, personalization-service-account).
   - Use scopes + metadata tags (namespace labels) and enforce per-key quotas. That gives you both billing separation and ability to apply stricter SLOs per account.

3) Routing + key validation across regions:
   - Key validation is stateless: signatures on JWTs are validated by the region endpoint using the current public keys. We replicate public key material across regions with strong consistency; validation does not require a central call.
   - For data locality, use a routing policy that pins EU-origin traffic to eu-central endpoints; if you want failover, we recommend first-level routing to EU-only replicas and second-level fallback to compatible models in another region (explicitly opt-in).

4) Client direct calls / PKCE: we strongly discourage client apps holding long-lived keys. If you want occasional client->Redwood calls: 
   - Use PKCE + OAuth flows to get short-lived tokens, and limit scope severely (read-only embeddings or inference with strict rate limits).
   - Prefer token exchange via your backend if the call will access private data.

Attachments: I'm including a token-exchange-flow.drawio (simple flow diagram) and the redwood-auth-options.pdf has the Option A/B comparison in a single page.

Proposed next step: 60-min technical deep-dive including your security engineer + our security engineer + infra engineer. Wed Sep 9, 10am PT or Thu Sep 10, 2pm PT — does either work? We can also split into two 45-min sessions (auth + routing / embeddings).

Thanks —

Marissa Cole
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
